chapters.title: Chapter 2: Detecting Regimes: From Rules to Statistics

lessons.title: From Rules to Probabilities: An Introduction to Statistical Regime Models

body.text: A probability is what a threshold refuses to give you. 'The market is 73% likely to be in a stressed regime today' is a fundamentally more useful sentence than 'regime = stressed', and it costs nothing but a different way of thinking about the problem.

children.text: The previous lesson closed on a promise: stop picking better thresholds, start estimating a probability instead. This lesson makes that idea concrete, with a small worked example you can compute by hand, before Chapter 3 turns it into a full Hidden Markov Model fitted on real Nifty and Bank Nifty data.
From a Label to a Probability

Instead of assigning every day a fixed label, up or down, calm or extreme, a probabilistic model assigns a probability to each possible regime: P(up trend) = 0.82, P(down trend) = 0.18, and updates those numbers as new data arrives. Near a genuine turning point, the probability drifts gradually through 0.6, 0.5, 0.4 rather than snapping from 1 to 0 overnight. That drift is not a weakness, it is the model honestly reporting that the evidence is genuinely mixed on that day, something a binary flag is structurally incapable of expressing.

body.title: Illustrative: Binary Trend Flag vs Smoothed Regime Probability, Weeks 1 to 12 of a Choppy Stretch

body.text: Both series above are stylized illustrations built to make the shape of the difference visible, not output from an actual fitted model. Chapter 3 produces the real version of the probability curve from data.

children.text: Notice the binary flag flips five times across these twelve weeks, each one a hard, instantaneous decision. The probability series never flips instantaneously; it drifts down through the uncertain middle weeks and only spends real time near the extremes when the evidence is actually one-sided. That is the whipsaw problem from the previous lesson, resolved not by a smarter threshold but by not thresholding at all until you actually need a single number for a downstream decision.
The Key Idea: Regimes Are Hidden, Not Observed

Here is the conceptual shift underneath everything in Chapter 3. You never actually observe 'the regime.' You observe prices, returns, and volatility, noisy signals that were generated by some underlying market state you cannot see directly. The job of a statistical regime model is to work backward from what is observable to a belief about what is hidden. A model built explicitly around this idea, an unobserved state generating observable data, with the state itself evolving from one period to the next, is called a Hidden Markov Model, the subject of the next chapter.
A Toy Example: Updating a Belief With Bayes' Rule

The simplest possible version of this updating process is a single application of Bayes' rule. You start with a prior belief about which regime you are in, observe one new data point, and update your belief using how likely that observation is under each regime.

body.caption: Bayes' rule: the posterior probability of regime R given a new observation x

children.text: Suppose your prior belief, based on how rare high-volatility days have been recently, is P(high-vol regime) = 0.20 and P(calm regime) = 0.80. Today Nifty falls 2.5%. A move that large has a likelihood of only 0.02 under the calm regime, but a likelihood of 0.15 under the high-vol regime, since big moves are simply more common there. Bayes' rule combines these into a posterior belief.

body.caption: One Bayesian update after observing a -2.5% day

body.label: What one extreme return did to the belief
body.context: A single -2.5% day moved the probability of being in a high-vol regime from a 1-in-5 prior to a better-than-even posterior. No threshold was crossed; the belief simply updated in proportion to the evidence.

children.text: What Chapter 3 Adds on Top of This Toy Example

This toy example hand-picked every number: the prior, and both likelihoods. A real Hidden Markov Model replaces each hand-picked piece with something estimated from data, and repeats the update every single day instead of once.

body.caption: From this toy example to Chapter 3's Hidden Markov Model

cells: A fixed prior, chosen by us (0.20)
A transition matrix: a persistence-aware prior for tomorrow, built from today's posterior and a self-transition probability learned from data, formalizing Chapter 1's E[duration] = 1/(1-p)
Fitted emission distributions: the actual statistical shape of returns under each regime, estimated from historical data
One manual update, for one day
The forward-backward algorithm and the Viterbi algorithm, updating and decoding probabilities across an entire price history at once
The number of hidden states itself, chosen using AIC or BIC rather than guessed

body.text: None of this added complexity is decoration. Every piece Chapter 3 introduces answers a specific weakness this chapter measured directly: the fitted emission distribution replaces an arbitrary threshold, the continuously updated probability replaces a whipsawing binary flag, and the learned transition matrix replaces a hand-picked confirmation window. You are not adding machinery for its own sake. You are finally giving each weak point in this chapter a proper fix instead of a patch.

body.title: Running Your Own Bayesian Update
body.prompt: Your prior belief is P(stressed regime) = 0.30. Today's realized volatility reading has a likelihood of 0.05 under the calm regime and 0.25 under the stressed regime. What is the posterior probability of the stressed regime, as a percentage?
body.explanation: P(observation) = (0.05 × 0.70) + (0.25 × 0.30) = 0.035 + 0.075 = 0.110. Posterior P(stressed | observation) = 0.075 / 0.110 ≈ 68.2%. A single volatility reading moved the belief from a 30% prior to a 68.2% posterior.

body.title: What 'Hidden' Means Here
body.question: In the context of a Hidden Markov Model for market regimes, what exactly is 'hidden'?
options: The daily returns and volatility, which are kept secret from the model
The regime itself, which is never directly observed and must be inferred from returns and volatility
The moving average window length, which is optimized in secret
The India VIX level, which is only published with a delay
body.explanation: The regime, calm, trending, stressed, and so on, is the hidden state. It is never directly labeled in the data. Returns, volatility, and other observable signals are generated by that hidden state, and the model's job is to infer the state from them, exactly the reasoning behind the toy Bayesian update in this lesson.

children.text: That closes Chapter 2. You now have working rule-based flags, a precise, measured account of why they break down, and the conceptual bridge to a genuinely different approach. Chapter 3 builds the real thing: a Hidden Markov Model fitted on Nifty returns, with transition matrices and emission distributions estimated from data instead of hand-picked.

points: A probabilistic regime model outputs a probability for each regime, which updates gradually as evidence accumulates, instead of a binary flag that jumps instantly
The core conceptual shift is treating the regime as hidden: never directly observed, only inferred from observable signals like returns and volatility
Bayes' rule is the basic mechanism for that inference: combine a prior belief with the likelihood of a new observation under each regime to get a posterior belief
A single extreme observation can move a regime probability sharply, in this lesson's example from a 20% prior to a 65.2% posterior after one large return

A Hidden Markov Model formalizes this toy example: a learned transition matrix replaces the fixed prior, fitted emission distributions replace hand-picked likelihoods, and the Viterbi and forward-backward algorithms replace a single manual update
